learning_objectives: Explain the core ideas of planning at Undergraduate Year 2 depth.
Apply planning concepts to worked examples and problems.
Critically discuss how planning connects to real-world practice in artificial intelligence.
lessons.reading_material:
Classical planning, STRIPS-style representations, and plan search for multi-step goals.

A brief note on why Planning earns a dedicated module in Artificial Intelligence. At this level, coursework is structured so that each topic does real conceptual work -- it either resolves a limitation of the previous topic, extends it to a broader class of cases, or introduces a method that later topics reuse. Understanding which of these roles Planning plays will make the rest of the module easier to follow.

The intended learning outcomes for this module are: Explain the core ideas of planning at Undergraduate Year 2 depth; Apply planning concepts to worked examples and problems; Critically discuss how planning connects to real-world practice in artificial intelligence. Treat these less as a checklist and more as a self-assessment tool: after working through the material, try to satisfy each outcome without reference to your notes, and any outcome you cannot satisfy cleanly marks exactly where to focus your remaining study time.

Central terminology for this module: Planning. A useful habit at this stage of study is to maintain your own running glossary rather than relying on recognising terms in context; being asked to produce a definition cold, without the surrounding sentence to lean on, is a much better test of whether a concept has actually been internalised.

Students frequently underestimate how much of the difficulty in material like this is conceptual rather than computational: getting the right numeric answer to a problem is not the same as being able to explain, in your own words and without notes, why the method used was appropriate. Assessment at this level increasingly rewards the latter, so it is worth practising explanation, not just calculation, as you work through the material.

To consolidate this module, work through the following: Guided worked example on planning; Small-group discussion / problem set on planning. Treat this as a diagnostic as much as an exercise: wherever it exposes a gap in your understanding, that gap is exactly where additional study time is best spent, rather than spreading review evenly across material you have already mastered.

The associated assignment is: Write a short summary connecting planning to one real-world example. Beyond satisfying the requirement, use it as an opportunity to surface exactly which parts of the module you can apply confidently and which parts you can only recognise -- that distinction is the most useful information you can extract from any assignment.

For review before assessment: Review planning before moving to the next module. A strong test of readiness is being able to reconstruct the core argument of this module from a blank page, in your own words and without consulting notes; if you can do that fluently, recognition-based review is no longer the most valuable use of your remaining study time.

To close, treat mastery of Planning as an ongoing project rather than a one-time task completed when the module ends. The strongest students in any Artificial Intelligence course are distinguished less by innate ability than by the habit of returning to earlier material once later material makes its relevance clearer -- make a note to revisit this module once you have progressed further in the course.

It is worth situating Planning within Artificial Intelligence before working through the material. Topics at this level are rarely self-contained; Planning both depends on concepts introduced earlier in the course and sets up reasoning that later modules will assume you already have available. Treating it as an isolated fact to memorise, rather than a piece of a larger argument, is the single most common reason students find later material harder than it needs to be.

Planning sits at a point in Artificial Intelligence where genuine understanding pays off disproportionately: it is referenced, directly or indirectly, in a wide range of subsequent material. Students who treat it as a box to check tend to find themselves relearning it under time pressure later; students who invest in understanding it now tend to find later modules noticeably more tractable.

A recurring failure mode at this level is superficial pattern-matching: recognising the surface features of a problem that resembles one seen in lecture and reproducing a memorised procedure, without having understood the underlying reasoning well enough to notice when the surface resemblance is misleading. The corrective habit is to ask, for every worked example, not just 'what was done' but 'why was this the right thing to do, and under what conditions would it stop being the right thing to do.'

real_world_examples: How 'Aggregate Demand & Supply' shows up in real-world economics practice: Modelling the whole economy's output and price level together.
How 'Fiscal Policy' shows up in real-world economics practice: How government spending and taxation influence the economy.

How 'Labor Economics' shows up in real-world economics practice: Studies labor supply and demand, human capital investment, wage inequality, discrimination, and the effects of minimum wages and unions on employment.

How 'Industrial Organization' shows up in real-world economics practice: Examines firm strategy and market power, covering oligopoly models, entry deterrence, product differentiation, and the economics of antitrust policy.
